content.statement: A LEFT JOIN returns every row of the left table, including rows that have no match in the right table.

remember: LEFT JOIN keeps every left row; when nothing matches, the right table's columns are NULL.

content.prompt: Each customer has zero or more orders. Which FROM clause lists every customer, including customers without orders?

options.text: FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
FROM orders o LEFT JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
FROM customers c RIGHT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id

remember: The table whose rows must all appear goes on the left side of a LEFT JOIN.

content.prompt: What does this query return?

remember: LEFT JOIN repeats a left row once per match and keeps an unmatched left row once, with NULLs.

content.prompt: The report should list every customer with their number of orders placed since 1 January 2026, showing 0 for customers without any. Find the bug.
content.code:
SELECT c.id,
       c.name,
       count(o.id) AS orders_2026
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
  ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.created_at >= DATE '2026-01-01'
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY c.name;

fixes.text: Change count(o.id) to count(*)
Move the date condition into the ON clause
Add OR o.created_at IS NULL to the WHERE clause

remember: A WHERE condition on the right table of a LEFT JOIN removes the NULL rows; put such filters in the ON clause.

content.statement: Adding more indexes to a table makes INSERTs into that table faster.

remember: Every index must be updated on each write, so indexes speed up reads but slow down inserts.

content.prompt: Which column is the weakest candidate for a B-tree index that serves WHERE column = value lookups?

options.text: orders.customer_id, a handful of rows per customer
users.is_active, true for about half the rows

remember: An index pays off when a lookup returns a small share of the rows; a column with two common values rarely benefits.

content.prompt: There is a B-tree index on users(email). Which WHERE condition is the odd one out because it cannot use that index?

remember: An index on a column does not cover an expression on it; to search by lower(email), index lower(email).

content.prompt: Match each PostgreSQL EXPLAIN node with what it does.

right.text: Collects matching row locations from an index first, then reads table pages in physical order
Returns the needed columns straight from the index, mostly without reading the table
Reads every row of the table
Finds each match in the index, then fetches that row from the table

remember: Seq Scan reads everything; Index Scan and Bitmap Heap Scan find rows through an index; Index Only Scan can skip the table.

content.statement: Loading 50 posts and then running one query per post to fetch its author sends 51 queries to the database.

remember: One query for the list plus one per item is N+1; load the related rows with a join or one batched query.

content.prompt: This code shows 20 orders with their customers. Which change removes the N+1 problem?

options.text: Start all 20 customer queries at once with Promise.all
Join customers in the first query and remove the loop
Run the loop on a single reused database connection

remember: Running the per-item queries in parallel is still N+1; one join or one batched query removes the extra round trips.

content.prompt: Fill the blank so all customers load in one query. The PostgreSQL driver sends ids as an integer array.

remember: Batch-load related rows with one query over all their ids, such as WHERE id = ANY($1) in PostgreSQL.

content.prompt: listPosts takes seconds in production although every single query is fast. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Run the getAuthor calls in parallel with Promise.all
Fetch the authors with a join in the posts query
Cache authors in a Map so each one is fetched once

remember: A query hidden in a helper still runs once per loop iteration; an await on a query inside a loop is the N+1 smell.

content.statement: When a transaction is rolled back, the changes made by its earlier, successful statements are undone as well.

remember: A transaction is all or nothing: ROLLBACK undoes every change made since BEGIN.

content.prompt: A transfer runs two UPDATEs between BEGIN and COMMIT. The server crashes after the first UPDATE, before COMMIT. What is in the database after the restart?

options.text: Both UPDATEs, replayed from the log
The first UPDATE, marked as pending

remember: Work that was not committed before a crash is discarded on restart; a half-done transaction never survives.

content.prompt: Match each ACID property with its guarantee.

right.text: Concurrent transactions do not see each other's uncommitted work
All statements take effect, or none do
Each transaction leaves the data satisfying every constraint

remember: Atomic: all or nothing. Consistent: constraints hold. Isolated: no interference. Durable: commits survive crashes.

content.prompt: DEBIT_SQL subtracts the amount from a balance and CREDIT_SQL adds it. After a transfer fails with Insufficient funds, the money has still left the sender's account. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Send ROLLBACK instead of COMMIT in the catch block
Move throw err above the COMMIT in the catch block
Add FOR UPDATE to the balance SELECT

remember: On any error inside a transaction, send ROLLBACK; a COMMIT after an application error saves the half-done work.

content.statement: Copying a customer's email into every order row, instead of storing it once in a customers table, is an example of normalization.

remember: Normalization stores each fact once; copying it into many rows is denormalization, and the copies can drift apart.

content.prompt: Every order row stores the customer's email. A customer changes their email and only their newest order is updated. What is this problem called?

remember: When one fact is stored in many rows, updating only some of them is an update anomaly.

content.prompt: Order the normal forms from least to most strict.

remember: Each normal form includes the one before it: 1NF, then 2NF, 3NF and BCNF.

content.prompt: Three of these tables break a normal form. Which one is the odd one out because it is in third normal form?

items.text: order_items(order_id, product_id, qty, product_name) with PK (order_id, product_id)
enrollments(student_id, course_id, grade) with PK (student_id, course_id)
users(id, phone_numbers) with PK (id), where phone_numbers holds a comma-separated list

remember: Every non-key column should depend on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.

content.statement: In SQL, the expression NULL = NULL evaluates to true.

remember: Any comparison with NULL, even NULL = NULL, yields NULL (unknown); test for it with IS NULL.

content.prompt: In some rows the discount column is NULL. What does price - discount return for those rows?

remember: Arithmetic with NULL gives NULL; use coalesce(discount, 0) when a missing value should count as 0.

content.prompt: What does this query return?

remember: count(*) counts rows; count(column), avg and the other aggregates skip NULLs.

content.prompt: The query should return verified users that were never deleted, but it returns no rows. Find the bug.
content.code:
SELECT id,
       email
FROM users
WHERE email_verified = true
  AND deleted_at = NULL
ORDER BY id;

fixes.text: Write deleted_at IS NULL
Write deleted_at = 'NULL'
Write deleted_at == NULL

remember: column = NULL is never true; use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL.

content.statement: WHERE filters rows before they are grouped, and HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY.

remember: Filter rows with WHERE before grouping; filter on aggregates such as count(*) with HAVING after grouping.

content.prompt: Why does PostgreSQL reject this query?

options.text: count(*) needs a column name in the parentheses
GROUP BY must also list count(*)
dept must also be wrapped in an aggregate
name is neither grouped nor aggregated

remember: A selected column must be in GROUP BY or inside an aggregate (unless a grouped primary key determines it); a group holds many values for it.

content.prompt: It should show, per city, how many different customers have at least one paid order. Find the bug.
content.code:
SELECT c.city,
       count(*) AS buyers
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o
  ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status = 'paid'
GROUP BY c.city
ORDER BY buyers DESC;

fixes.text: Use count(o.customer_id) instead of count(*)
Use LEFT JOIN orders instead of JOIN
Use count(DISTINCT c.id) instead of count(*)

remember: After a join, count(*) counts joined rows; use count(DISTINCT key) to count distinct entities.

content.prompt: What does this query return?
content.code:
WITH sales(region, amount) AS (
  VALUES ('north', 100), ('north', 300),
         ('south', 50),  ('south', 60),
         ('east', 500)
)
SELECT region, count(*) AS n
FROM sales
WHERE amount > 55
GROUP BY region
HAVING count(*) > 1
ORDER BY region;

remember: WHERE removes rows before they are counted; HAVING then removes whole groups.

content.statement: A scalar subquery in the SELECT list must return at most one row.

remember: A scalar subquery that returns several rows is an error; one that returns no rows gives NULL.

content.prompt: Which WHERE clause makes SELECT * FROM customers c return only the customers that have at least one order?

options.text: WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)
WHERE c.id IN (SELECT id FROM orders)
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id IS NOT NULL)

remember: EXISTS needs a condition linking the subquery to the outer row; without one it is true for every row.

content.prompt: What does this query return?

remember: x NOT IN (a list containing NULL) is never true; use NOT EXISTS when the subquery column can be NULL.

content.prompt: banned.user_id can be NULL. Fill the blank so the query returns every user who is not banned.
content.code:
SELECT u.id, u.email
FROM users u
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM banned b
  WHERE ____
);

remember: NOT EXISTS with an equality to the outer row means no matching row exists, and NULLs cannot break it.

content.statement: A PRIMARY KEY column may hold NULL in one row, as long as no other row is NULL too.

remember: A primary key is UNIQUE plus NOT NULL: every row needs a value, and no two rows may share it.

content.prompt: In PostgreSQL, the users table has UNIQUE (email) with default settings. Two rows are inserted with email set to NULL. What happens?

options.text: The second insert fails with a unique violation
The first insert fails, since UNIQUE implies NOT NULL
Both rows get an empty string instead of NULL

remember: UNIQUE treats NULLs as distinct by default, so many NULLs are allowed; add NOT NULL or NULLS NOT DISTINCT to stop that.

content.prompt: Fill the blank so every order must belong to an existing customer.

remember: A column-level foreign key is written REFERENCES table (column); the database then rejects ids that do not exist.

content.prompt: Match each constraint with the rule it enforces.

right.text: Rejects rows for which a condition is false
Identifies each row; implies UNIQUE and NOT NULL
Non-NULL values must exist in the referenced table
No two rows may share the same non-NULL value

remember: PRIMARY KEY identifies rows, FOREIGN KEY points to existing rows, UNIQUE forbids duplicates, CHECK tests a condition.

content.statement: Under READ COMMITTED, a transaction can read changes that another transaction has made but not yet committed.

remember: READ COMMITTED never shows uncommitted changes; reading them is a dirty read, which PostgreSQL never allows.

content.prompt: In PostgreSQL at READ COMMITTED, two transactions run UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 10 WHERE id = 1 at the same time. What happens?

options.text: Both read the original balance, so the second overwrites the first and one deduction is lost
The second UPDATE fails with a serialization error
The second UPDATE waits for the first to commit, then subtracts from the new balance
The second UPDATE reads the first one's uncommitted balance without waiting

remember: An UPDATE that computes from the current value is safe: a concurrent update of the same row waits, then re-reads it.

content.prompt: Order the SQL standard isolation levels from weakest to strongest.

remember: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE: each level rules out more anomalies.

content.prompt: When two customers buy the same product at the same moment, stock sometimes drops by 1 instead of 2. Concurrent purchases should run one after the other. Find the bug (PostgreSQL, READ COMMITTED).

fixes.text: Append FOR SHARE to the SELECT
Append FOR KEY SHARE to the SELECT
Append FOR UPDATE to the SELECT

remember: Lock rows you read and then overwrite with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE; FOR SHARE can deadlock, and FOR KEY SHARE does not block the UPDATE.

content.statement: ORDER BY is evaluated after the SELECT list, so it can use a column alias defined in SELECT.

remember: SELECT runs after WHERE and before ORDER BY, so an alias works in ORDER BY but not in WHERE.

content.prompt: Why does this query fail?

options.text: WHERE runs before SELECT, so line_total does not exist yet
An alias must be written in double quotes to be referenced
Aliases cannot be given to calculated columns
Filters on calculated values must use HAVING instead

remember: WHERE runs before SELECT; repeat the expression or filter in an outer query to use an alias.

content.prompt: Put these clauses in the order SQL logically evaluates them.

remember: Logical order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT.

content.prompt: What does this query return?
content.code:
WITH sales(rep, amount) AS (
  VALUES ('ana', 50), ('ben', 70), ('ana', 45),
         ('cid', 35), ('ben', 30), ('cid', 55)
)
SELECT rep, sum(amount) AS total
FROM sales
WHERE amount > 30
GROUP BY rep
ORDER BY total DESC
LIMIT 1;

remember: LIMIT is applied last, to the sorted groups; WHERE removed rows before they were summed.

content.statement: A regular (non-materialized) view stores a copy of its result rows.

remember: A view is a saved query that runs each time it is used; only a materialized view stores rows.

content.prompt: What is a common reason to create a regular view?

options.text: To cache the query's result rows so that later reads get faster
To give a complex query a name and reuse it like a table
To keep a backup copy of a table
To add an index to a query

remember: Views name and reuse queries and can hide columns; they do not cache data or speed queries up by themselves.

content.prompt: What does the last statement return?

options.text: An error: the view must be refreshed first

remember: A regular view runs its query on every use, so it always reflects the current table rows.

content.prompt: In PostgreSQL, three of these are true of a materialized view. Which one is the odd one out because it is false?

items.text: It stores its result rows on disk
It can have indexes of its own
REFRESH ... CONCURRENTLY needs a unique index on it
It updates itself whenever a base table changes

remember: A materialized view is a stored snapshot: it can be indexed, and it changes only on REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW.

content.prompt: What does this query return?
content.code:
WITH users(id, name) AS (
  VALUES (1, 'Ana')
), orders(user_id, total) AS (
  VALUES (1, 100), (1, 50)
), logins(user_id, day) AS (
  VALUES (1, 'mon'), (1, 'tue'), (1, 'wed')
)
SELECT u.name,
       sum(o.total) AS revenue,
       count(l.day) AS logins
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
LEFT JOIN logins l ON l.user_id = u.id
GROUP BY u.name;

remember: Joining two one-to-many tables to the same row multiplies their rows; aggregate each one in its own subquery before joining.

content.prompt: Fill the blank so the index hands this query its 20 rows already sorted, without reading entries it then throws away.
content.code:
SELECT id, total
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = $1
  AND status = 'paid'
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;

CREATE INDEX orders_paid_feed
  ON orders (____);

remember: In a composite index put the equality columns first and the sort or range column last, so matching rows come out in order.

content.prompt: A batching loader (DataLoader style) removes the N+1 when 20 resolvers each need one author. Put its steps in order.

steps.text: Send one query with WHERE id = ANY($1)
Each resolver calls load(authorId) and gets a promise
Resolve each waiting promise with its own author
Wait for the current tick to end, collecting every requested id
Put the returned rows in a map keyed by id

remember: A batching loader collects the ids asked for in one tick, loads them with one query and maps the rows back by id, not by position.

content.prompt: In PostgreSQL the coupon INSERT fails. Fill the blank so order 7 and the audit row are still committed together.

remember: After an error, ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT undoes only the work since the savepoint; in PostgreSQL nothing else runs in the transaction until you do.

content.prompt: order_items.unit_price is copied from products.price at checkout. A reviewer says it duplicates products.price and should be replaced with a join. Which reply is right?

options.text: Agree: a join keeps one source of truth for every price
Keep it: it is the price at the time of sale, a separate fact from today's price
Keep it, but update it in every order whenever products.price changes
Agree: the same column in two tables breaks third normal form

remember: A copied value is redundant only if it is the same fact; the price paid at checkout is its own fact and must not follow later price changes.

content.prompt: opt_out is a nullable boolean that stays NULL until the user chooses. The newsletter should reach every confirmed user who has not opted out, but users who never chose get nothing. Find the bug.
content.code:
SELECT id, email
FROM users
WHERE confirmed
  AND opt_out <> true
ORDER BY id;

fixes.text: Write opt_out = false
Write NOT opt_out
Write opt_out IS NOT TRUE

remember: For a NULL value, <> true, = false and NOT all give unknown and drop the row; IS NOT TRUE or coalesce(opt_out, false) keeps it.

content.prompt: It should list customers who have orders but never paid for any of them. It returns no rows, although such customers exist. Find the bug.
content.code:
SELECT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
HAVING count(CASE WHEN o.status = 'paid'
                  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = 0
ORDER BY c.name;

fixes.text: Change JOIN to LEFT JOIN
Remove ELSE 0 from the CASE
Add WHERE o.status = 'paid' and use HAVING count(*) = 0

remember: count() counts every non-NULL value, 0 included; count a condition with count(*) FILTER (WHERE ...) or a CASE without ELSE.

content.prompt: What does this query return?

options.text: An error: column id does not exist in banned

remember: A column the subquery's own tables lack silently refers to the outer query; qualify columns in subqueries, as in b.user_id.

content.prompt: A double click on Sign up sometimes creates two users with the same email. Find the bug (PostgreSQL, READ COMMITTED).

fixes.text: Declare email text NOT NULL UNIQUE
Append FOR UPDATE to the SELECT 1 query
Open the transaction with BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ

remember: Only a UNIQUE constraint stops concurrent duplicates; a check before INSERT cannot lock a row that does not exist yet.

content.prompt: Match each concurrency anomaly with what happens.

right.text: Two transactions each check a rule, then update different rows, and together break it
Re-running the same WHERE query returns extra rows another transaction inserted
Reading data that another transaction has not committed yet
The same row, read twice, has changed because another transaction committed an update

remember: Dirty read sees uncommitted data, non-repeatable read sees a row change, phantom read sees new rows, write skew breaks a rule across rows.

content.prompt: What does this query return?
content.code:
WITH posts(id, likes) AS (
  VALUES (1, 5), (2, 9), (3, 0),
         (4, 7), (5, 3)
)
SELECT id, count(*) OVER () AS total
FROM posts
WHERE likes > 0
ORDER BY likes DESC
LIMIT 2;

remember: Window functions run after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING but before ORDER BY and LIMIT, so count(*) OVER () counts the rows before paging.

content.prompt: In PostgreSQL, three of these are true. Which one is the odd one out because it is false?

items.text: A plain REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW blocks readers until done
A WHERE on a view can still use the table's indexes
A view made with SELECT * picks up columns added later
A table cannot be dropped while a view uses it, without CASCADE

remember: PostgreSQL expands SELECT * when a view is created, so columns added to the table later need CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW.
